The paraneoplastic syndrome commonly seen in squamous cell lung carcinoma is parathyroid-like hormone production, which leads to hypercalcemia. → Laryngeal squamous carcinoma (choice D) can cause cough, hoarseness, weight loss, and is also associated with cigarette smoking. But lung cancers are far more common than laryngeal cancers, and SIADH is very suggestive of oat cell lung carcinoma. → Lung adenocarcinoma (choice E) has been recognized as the common type of lung cancer is non-smokers and is not commonly associated with SIADH. Key point: The combination of cough, hoarseness, weight loss, and SIADH in an old patient heavy smoker  is suggestive of small cell lung carcinoma also known as oat cell lung carcinoma.

subject: Medicine
question: A 27-year-old male presents to your department because he has been coughing up bloody sputum for the past 5 days. His past medical history is significant for recurrent rhinitis and sinusitis for many years, but according to the patient, they have been more frequent in the past 2 years. On physical examination saddle nose deformity is noted. Hematuria is observed on urinalysis. Further work-up reveals positive cytoplasmic anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: This patient presents with hemoptysis and hematuria, which suggest pulmonary and renal disease. Given the patient’s history of recurrent rhinitis and sinusitis and the positive cytoplasmic antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, the most likely diagnosis is granulomatosis with polyangiitis (choice B) formerly known as Wegener’s granulomatosis. It is a multisystem autoimmune disease of unknown etiology characterized by necrotizing granulomatous inflammation and pauci-immune vasculitis in small- and medium-sized blood vessels. Diagnosis is generally confirmed with tissue biopsy from a site of active disease; renal and lung biopsies are most specific for granulomatosis  with polyangiitis. → Churg-Strauss syndrome (choice A) is an allergic granulomatous angiitis that presents with asthma, paranasal sinusitis, and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis. Eosinophilia is a common finding and perinuclear-ANCA (antimyeloperoxidase antibodies) are better diagnostic markers than c-ANCA. → Goodpasture’s syndrome (choice C) causes acute glomerulonephritis and pulmonary hemorrhage due to the presence of circulating anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies. → Sarcoidosis (choice D) a multisystem inflammatory disease of unknown etiology that manifests as noncaseating granulomas, predominantly in the lungs and intra-thoracic lymph nodes. Black people have increased risk of developing this disease. It is not associated with cytoplasmic anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies. → Cryoglobulinemia (choice E) is characterized by the presence of cryoglobulins in the serum. Cryoglobulins are single or mixed immunoglobulins that undergo reversible precipitation at low temperatures. Studies have shown close association of this condition with Hepatitis C. Key point: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is a multisystem necrotizing granulomatous inflammation that often presents with respiratory and renal involvement with symptoms such as hemoptysis and hematuria. Cytoplasmic anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies are commonly present and biopsy is diagnostic of this condition. Wegener

subject: Medicine
topic: Abnormal ECG with pleuritic chest pain
question: A 52-year-old male presents to your department with pleuritic chest pain. ECG shows:
explanation:
This patient has pleuritic chest pain and EKG changes with ST elevation in all leads except aVR and V1, which is characteristic of acute pericarditis (choice E). Another significant finding in this inflammatory condition of the pericardium is a friction rub. Below is an image that highlights the leads that are usually abnormal in acute pericarditis: all leads have an ST elevation except for aVR, V1, and sometimes III.

It should be noted here that this EKG presentation is only seen in stage 1 of acute pericarditis. In stage 2, the ST segments return to normal and there’s a T wave flattening. Stage 3 is characterized by T wave inversion, and finally in stage 4 there’s a resolution of T wave inversion. The progression from one stage to another is variable and may take hours to days to weeks. → Pulmonary embolism (choice A) is characterized by the McGinn-White sign in an S1Q3T3 pattern. → Myocardial infarction (choice B) causes ST elevations that could be confused with some aspects of EKG findings of acute pericarditis but it does not cause pleuritic chest pain. → Ventricular aneurysm (choice C), has an EKG presentation that can sometimes be confused with anterior myocardial infarction due to ST elevations in V1-V4 leads. Therefore, in a patient with an old myocardial infarction, it is important to recognize the distinction. According to the American Journal of Medicine the T/QRS ratio can help distinguish the two, with this ration being high in acute myocardial infarction ( > 0.36) but low in ventricular aneurysm. For example in a patient with a T wave equal to 1 square and QRS of 11 squares, the ratio would be 1/11= 0.09, this is < 0.36 and would be suggestive of a ventricular aneurysm from an old MI instead of a new anterior myocardial infarction. → Digoxin toxicity (choice D) presents with a classic “scooped out” ST segment depression, prolonged PR interval, and short QT interval. It also causes sinus bradycardia. Key point: Stage 1 of acute pericarditis is associated with an EKG that shows elevated ST segments in all leads except aVR, V1, and III.

subject: Medicine
question: A 47-year-old female is brought to your department with fever, altered mental status and petechial rash over her upper and lower extremities for the last 48 hours. On physical examination petechial rash is noted, mild jaundice, and splenomegaly. Her laboratory tests show: Hemoglobin: 90 g/L Platelet count: 17 - 109/L PT : 12 sec aPTT: 32 seconds Reticulocyte count: 10% Bilirubin: 32 micromol/L Direct bilirubin: 4 micromol/L Fibrinogen: normal BUN: 20 mmol/L Creatinine: 150 micromol/L LDH: 845 U/L Blood smear: numerous schistocytes What would be the most appropriate next step in the treatment of this patient?
explanation: This patient’s history of present illness combined with her laboratory tests demonstrate the 5 key characteristics of thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) namely, fever, mental status changes, renal impairment, hemolytic anemia, and thrombocytopenia. The fibrinogen and coagulation times are normal, which should be useful to exclude the possibility of disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC). Patients with TTP have unusually large multimers of von Willebrand factor (vWF) in their plasma. Patients with TTP lack ADAMTS 13, a plasma protease that is responsible for the breakdown of these ultralarge vWF multimers. The therapy of choice for TTP is plasma exchange (plasmapheresis) with fresh frozen plasma (choice E). Usually, at least 5 plasma exchanges are performed in the first 10 days. Plasmapheresis has reduced mortality from 90% to 15%. It allows removal of autoantibody and repletes ADAMTS13. → Renal dialysis (choice A) is effective in children with hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS), which has some similarities with TTP, but it is not the best treatment to manage this patient. → Aspirin and dipyridamole (choice B) used to be part of standard therapy added on plasmapheresis and fresh frozen plasma but they have fallen out of favor. Both of these would not be effective in treating this patient without plasmapheresis. → Platelet transfusion (choice C) should be avoided in TTP patients. There have been reports of myocardial infarction and stroke following platelet transfusion. → High-molecular weight von Willebrand (choice D) in patients who have ADAMTS 13 deficiency, such as TTP patients, is pathogenic and it would not be an appropriate treatment for this patient. Key point: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura is characterized by mental status changes, fever, renal impairment, hemolytic anemia, and thrombocytopenia. It is best treated with plasmapheresis and fresh frozen plasma.

subject: Medicine
question: A 37-year-old female with a history of asthma and hypertension presents to your department for a follow-up. She reports that recently her BP measurements at the local drug store have been consistently around 170/100 mmHg. She denies shortness of breath, wheezing, chest pain, and cough. In the past she had developed angioedema after treatment with lisinopril. She has a history of sulfa allergies. What would be the most appropriate medication to control this patient’s blood pressure?
explanation: This question is very straightforward: knowing the mechanism of action of anti-hypertensive medications and their contraindications, which of these drugs is most likely to be beneficial in a patient with asthma history? The correct answer is amlodipine (choice B). It is a calcium channel blocker that reduces blood pressure through vasodilation. It is a long acting drug usually given once a day as its effects can last for many hours, gradually decreasing blood pressure to the appropriate levels. This makes it more preferable than, say, nifedipine, especially the short-acting form of that drug, as it tends to dramatically decrease blood pressure in a way that could result in sudden hypoperfusion of vital organs and cause serious side effects. → Propranolol (choice A) and Carvedilol (choice D) are non-selective beta-blockers, that is, they block both beta-1 and beta-2 receptors, which could result in serious bronchoconstriction in asthmatic patients. → Hydrochlorothiazide (choice C) is a diuretic that contains sulfonamide functional group and could cause sulfa cross- allergy. → Enalapril (choice E) should be avoided because the patient has developed angioedema with lisinopril. Though the drugs are different, the mechanism of action is the same and is linked to the vasoactive peptide bradykinin, which is normally broken down by ACE, but is elevated inappropriately in predisposed patients when this enzyme is inhibited by these drugs. Key point: Nonselective beta-blockers are contraindicated in asthmatics. Many thiazides have cross-allergenicity with other sulfa- drugs and should be avoided in patients with sulfa-allergies. If a patient has angioedema with one type of ACE inhibitors, all ACE inhibitors should be avoided in that patient.

subject: Medicine
question: A 32-year-old male presents to your department with complaints of right knee pain for 1 week. It is located at the lateral aspect of the joint and is worsened by running downhill and climbing stairs. He has been trying to lose weight with increased exercise such as cycling and running the last 2 months. Patient denies locking or popping of the knee. He states that the pain does not get worse by prolonged sitting. The patient has not had any accident or traumatic injury to his knee. Valgus and McMurray tests are normal. Noble and Ober tests are positive. Knee X-ray reveals no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
This patient presents with knee pain. The differential diagnosis of knee pain is very wide and for a proper diagnosis to be made it is important to clarify the characteristics of the pain, including its onset, location, duration, severity, and quality. Aggravating and alleviating factors also need to be identified. The description of the patient’s symptoms, his history, and the findings on physical examination are suggestive of iliotibial band syndrome (choice D). It is characterized by lateral knee pain that is localized over the lateral femoral epicondyle. The iliotibial band is a dense fibrous band of tissue that originates from the anterior superior iliac spine region and extends down the lateral portion of the thigh to the knee. The iliotibial band has insertions on the lateral tibial condyle and the distal portion of the femur. This condition is often caused by overuse and this is why it is the most common cause of lateral knee pain in runners, cyclists, and military recruits

undergoing basic training. Climbing stairs and running downhill make the pain worse. A positive Noble test is considered suggestive of the diagnosis. This consists of a varus stress applied to the knee flexed at 30 degrees. → Patello-femoral pain syndrome (choice A) presents with retropatellar knee pain that worsens with squatting and ascending stairs. Usual physical findings are localized around the knee. Tenderness is often present along the facets of the patella. When Noble test is said to be positive, the first diagnosis that should come to mind should be iliotibial band syndrome. → Osteoarthritis (choice B) is excluded by the normal X-ray results. → Pes anserine bursitis (choice C) is an inflammatory condition of the medial knee. It is also associated with knee overuse, and presents with pain, swelling, and tenderness over the inner knee. This differs from iliotibial band syndrome that present with lateral knee pain. → Lateral collateral ligament sprain (choice E) could cause knee pain with presentation almost similar to iliotibial band, but it is usually caused by injury of the lateral collateral ligament and is acute in onset. Key point: Iliotibial band syndrome is the most common cause of lateral knee pain among athletes. Positive Noble test is suggestive of this diagnosis.

subject: Medicine
question: A 58-year-old male presents to your department with complaints of severe pain on the right lateral side of the chest for the last 5 days. The patient says that it started feeling like tingling, then it got worse to the point that he could barely put a shirt on as the slightest touch of a shirt to his skin caused unbearable pain. Ibuprofen and acetaminophen have had minimal effect in reducing the pain. The patient denies cough, shortness of breath, trauma, and any pain felt internally. He reports that the pain is on his skin. The patient’s past medical history is significant for diabetes and ulcerative colitis. The patient had shingles about 3 weeks ago. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for his current condition?
explanation:
This patient’s pain started as paresthetic in nature and at this moment he is experiencing allodynia (a pain due to a stimulus which does not normally provoke pain). Given his recent acute herpes zoster reactivation in the form of shingles, his current symptoms are suggestive of postherpetic neuralgia. Herpes zoster (HZ) is a viral infection that usually presents as a childhood infection of varicella (chicken pox). Following the acute phase, the virus enters the sensory nervous system, where it is harbored in the geniculate, trigeminal, or dorsal root ganglia and remains dormant for many years. With advancing age or immunocompromised states, the virus reactivates and an eruption (shingles) occurs. Even after the acute rash subsides, pain can persist or recur in shingles-affected areas. This condition is known as postherpetic neuralgia and majority experience this condition in the 6 months following shingles. About 9% of patients may develop postherpetic

neuralgia 12 months after shingles. A number of treatments have been studied for the management of postherpetic neuralgia. Tricyclic antidepressants such as amitriptyline and noretriptylline, anticonvulsants such as gabapentin, and opioids such as morphine and tramadol, have been found to be effective in the treatment of postherpetic neuralgia. Nortriptylline (choice D) would be an appropriate treatment for this patient’s condition. → Famciclovir (choice A) and Bivudin (choice B) are antivirals that are used in the treatment of acute herpes zoster reactivation when shingles develop, but would not be effective in the treatment of postherpetic neuralgia. → Prednisone (choice C) has not been shown to be effective in the treatment of postherpetic neuralgia, however, it has been used as an adjunctive drug to anti-virals to speed recovery of shingles. → Carbamazepine (choice E) is an antiepileptic medication with sufficient evidence proving it is ineffective in the treatment of postherpetic neuralgia and is therefore not recommended to manage this patient’s condition.

Key point: Postherpetic neuralgia is a condition characterized by neuropathic pain days, weeks, to months after shingles. It can be treated with tricyclic antidepressants such as nortriptylline, antiepileptics such as gabapentin, and opioids such as tramadol.

subject: Medicine
question: A 20-year-old female presents to your department with difficulty speaking, excessive salivation, and clumsiness with the hands. She takes no medications except oral contraceptive pills. Family history is significant for a paternal uncle who had a similar condition and died at the age of 48. Physical examination reveals mild spasticity at the knees. Slit lamp examination shows a hyperpigmented ring around the iris. Liver function tests shows ALT: 108 U/L AST: 97 U/L After the patient's diagnosis is made and treatment is started, which of the following test would be the best to monitor therapy?
explanation:
The neurological symptoms described in this patient of difficulty speaking and clumsiness with the hands combined with the findings of spasticity at the knees, the Kayser-Fleischer ring noted on slit lamp examination, and the abnormal liver function tests all point to a diagnosis of Wilson disease. It is an autosomal recessive inheritance disease of the copper metabolism characterized by excessive deposition of copper in the liver, brain, and other tissues.

Out of the choices given, urinary copper excretion (choice D) would be the best way to confirm it. In untreated patients, the 24-hour urinary excretion of copper reflects the amount of non-ceruloplasmin-bound copper in the circulation. Normally urinary copper excretion should not exceed 40 microgram/day but in patients with Wilson disease urinary copper excretion is above 100 microgram/day. Chelating agents such as D-penicillamine are therefore prescribed to promote 24-hour excretion of approximately 2 mg of copper in the urine, to induce a negative copper balance. Regular measurement of the 24-hour urinary excretion of copper provides an important index of copper removal from the body. If the excretion level in a compliant patient decreases to less than 0.5 mg daily, the dose can be lowered. → Genetic testing (choice A) is impractical in Wilson disease due multiplicity of mutations involved; about 200 mutations of the ATP7B gene have been identified and currently there are no commercially available genetic testing. It is not the best follow up test. → Serum ceruloplasmin (choice B) is considered useful in patients with classic symptoms and the Kayser-Fleischer ring - It is the major carrier of copper in the blood but is also present as the protein without copper the copper. It is  an important test to order as initial test and in a patient with neurological symptoms it can point to the diagnosis; however, it is also an acute phase reactant that can increase in infections, hepatic inflammations, pregnancy, and estrogen use. It is also decreased in malnutrition, nephrotic syndrome, malabsorption, and protein-losing enteropathy. Serum ceruloplasmin levels would be unreliable in this patient, who is on oral contraceptive pills and is also not the best follow up test to monitor therapy. → Abdominal CT scan (choice C) is uninformative with findings neither specific nor sensitive for Wilson disease and would not be helpful as follow up test in a patient receiving therapy. → Cerebrospinal fluid studies (choice E) would not be useful in monitoring chelation therapy for Wilson disease in this patient. Key point: Wilson disease is an autosomal recessive inheritance disease of the copper metabolism characterized by excessive deposition of copper in the liver, brain, and other tissues. Wilson disease is treated with D-penicillamine, a copper chelating agent and the best test to monitor therapy is urinary copper excretion.

subject: Medicine
question: A 67-year-old female presents to your department with her husband and they report that she has been experiencing mood swings with unusually frequent irritability, decreased sleep need, racing thoughts, and excitation. The patient has a 4-year- history of rheumatoid arthritis and was recently started on a new medication. Which of the following is the most likely medication the patient is being treated with?
explanation:
This patient presents with psychiatric symptoms suggestive of a mania. Moods swings, irritability, decreased need to

sleep, racing thoughts, excitation, and other symptoms usually associated with bipolar disorder are seen in many patients treated with prednisone (choice D) or other corticosteroids, especially with doses higher than 40 mg per day. Psychiatric side effects associated with corticosteroids are reversible with discontinuation of the drug or significant reduction in dose. Other common side effects of corticosteroids to be aware of are hypertension, hirsutism, obesity, diabetes mellitus, peptic ulcer disease, fatty liver, leukocytosis, oral candidiasis, myopathy, osteoporosis, and cataracts. → Gold salts (choice A) can cause coloring of the skin in shades of mauve to a purplish dark grey when exposed to sunlight, if the salts are taken on a regular basis over a long period of time. They can also cause kidney damage, pruritus, and oral ulcers. → Methotrexate (choice B) can cause ulcerative stomatitis, leukopenia with immunosuppression, pneumonitis, pulmonary fibrosis, dizziness, and kidney failure. → Meloxicam (choice C) like most NSAIDs can cause peptic ulcers, tinnitus, and skin rash. However, compared to other NSAIDs its side effects profile is favourable. → Minocycline (choice E) can cause diarrhea, photosensitivity, dizziness, lupus, blue-gray skin, and like other tetracyclines it can cause discoloration of teeth, especially in children. Key point: High dose corticosteroids can cause psychiatric adverse effects, particularly mood changes, which are reversible with discontinuation of the drug or significant reduction in dose.

subject: Medicine
question: A 76-year-old man is brought to your department by the police after he was found wandering on the street. The patient’s family was also notified and joined him shortly after. The patient reports that he has been having visual hallucinations, they are non-threatening in nature, and mainly are of the type of seeing objects in places where they are really not. His wife says that his mental abilities have deteriorated over the last 6 months. There are episodes he seems confused and unable to answer questions, though also he could be alert and coherent in his thinking. About 4 months ago he also started to be slow in his movements and has a shuffling gait. He also has occasional dizziness especially when he stands up to walk. On physical examination the patient appears well hydrated, his BP is 125/80 mmHg when seated and 100/65 mmHg when standing. His heart rate is 70 bpm, respirations 16/min, and temperature 37.4°C. A coarse resting tremor of the hands is noted bilaterally and persists on intentional movements. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
This patient presents with visual hallucination, fluctuations in cognitive function, Parkinson-like motor features, and orthostatic hypotension on physical examination, which all combined are suggestive of Lewy body dementia (choice E). It

is a progressive, degenerative dementia of unknown etiology. While the three core clinical features of (1) fluctuating cognition with pronounced variation in attention and alertness, (2) recurrent visual hallucinations (typically well formed and detailed), and (3) spontaneous features of parkinsonism are the basis for making the diagnosis, the final diagnosis can only be made after histopathological studies are done that demonstrate an eosinophilic round inclusion found in the cytoplasm of substantia nigra cells and in the nucleus basalis of Meynert, locus ceruleus, and dorsal raphe, as well as in the dorsal motor nucleus. → Parkinson’s disease (choice A) is incorrect. Dementia generally occurs late in Parkinson’s disease. Because Parkinson’s disease and Lewy body dementia have some similarities, an arbitrary period of 12 months has been determined as the length of time motor features of Parkinson’s disease have to be present before dementia symptoms present for the diagnosis of Parkinson’s disease to be preferred over Lewy body dementia. This patient’s dementia was noticed 6 months ago while Parkinson-like features were noticed 4 months ago. → Shy-Drager syndrome (choice B) also known as multiple system atrophy is a progressive neurodegenerative disease of undetermined etiology, with predominant parkinsonism and cerebellar features, and autonomic nervous dysfunction. In addition to parkinsonism, patients also present with cerebellar ataxia, erectile dysfunction, urinary incontinence or retention, and orthostatic hypotension. It can be easily differentiated from Parkinson’s disease when patients are found to be unresponsive to levodopa and autonomic dysfunction symptoms are significant. It can be differentiated from Lewy body dementia, because in the latter, cognitive function abnormalities usually present before Parkinson-like features. → Alzheimer’s disease (choice C) presents with dementia, but the findings on physical examination suggestive of Parkinsonism make this a less likely diagnosis compared to Lewy body dementia. → Normal pressure hydrocephalus (choice D) is characterized by Hakim’s triad of dementia, urinary incontinence, and gait disturbance. This patient’s clinical presentation is more suggestive of Lewy body dementia. Key point: Lewy body dementia is characterized by three core clinical features of  fluctuating cognition with pronounced variation in attention and alertness, recurrent visual hallucinations, and spontaneous features of parkinsonism.

subject: Medicine
question: A 72-year-old male presents to your department with complaints of prolonged constipation, early satiety, and gastroesophageal reflux. This has led to feeling bloated most of the time and weight loss. The patient was diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease 5 years ago and is treated with Selegiiline and Levodopa-Carbidopa combination. He was recently evaluated by his neurologist and found to be in stage 4 of the Hoehn and Yahr scale of this disease. Which of the following medication is contraindicated in this patient?
explanation:
This patient presents with constipation and symptoms suggestive of gastroparesis or delayed gastric emptying.

Gastrointestinal motility is reduced in Parkinson’s disease; besides, the medications used to treat this condition can also cause constipation. Patients can have hard, dry stools that are painful to pass due to slowed motility, and delayed emptying of a full bowel due to incoordination of rectal muscles. This could lead to complications such as paralytic ileus, acute bowel obstruction secondary to impaction, volvulus, and Ogilvie’s syndrome. Generally, metoclopramide (choice B) can be used to treat gastroparesis but it is contraindicated in patients with severe Parkinson’s disease such as this patient who was recently evaluated to be in stage 4 on the Hoehn and Yahr scale of this condition. Parkinson’s disease is characterized by loss of pigmented dopaminergic neurons and since this medication is a dopamine antagonist that crosses the brain blood barrier, it would worsen the patient’s condition. → Ropinirole (choice A) and Pramipexole (choice C) are non-ergoline dopamine agonists and they are used in the treatment of Parkinson’s disease. They are not contraindicated in this patient. → Domperidone (choice D) is a peripheral dopamine (D2) and (D3) receptor antagonist. Since it doesn’t cross the brain blood barrier like Metoclopramide, it is one of the few dopamine antagonists that can be used as prokinetic to increase gastrointestinal peristalsis and promote gastric emptying in this patient. → Isradipine (choice E) is a calcium channel blocker used as an antihypertensive medication that has been recently studied for use in treating Parkinson’s disease with promising initial results. It is not contraindicated in this patient. Key point: Metoclopramide is a dopamine antagonist and should not be used in patients with severe Parkinson's disease.

subject: Medicine
question: A 35-year-old male presents to your department with severe abdominal pain. He had similar complaints 3 months ago and after evaluation he was prescribed omeprazole for peptic ulcer disease. He says that the drug seemed to help a bit initially, but currently he feels his pain is getting worse. He says that the pain is associated with food. His father died at the age of 51 in a car accident. His mother is 58 years old and healthy. He has an older brother with a history of kidney stones. On physical examination he has pain in the epigastric region. Laboratory tests show: Sodium: 140 mmol/L Chloride: 116 mmol/L Potassium: 4.8 mmol/L Bicarbonate: 19 mmol/L Magnesium: 0.85 mmol/L Calcium: 3 mmol/L BUN: 7 mmol/L Creatinine: 200 microg/L Glucose: 5.5 mmol/L Gastrin: 1.1 ng/mL (normal < 100pg/mL) If MEN is suspected, which of the following would be the best choice to arrive at the correct diagnosis?
explanation: This patient’s abdominal pain is most likely caused by peptic ulcer disease. His history of abdominal pain, minimal relief with omeprazole, and the laboratory test results that reveal excessive levels of gastrin point to a gastrinoma (i.e.Zollinger- Ellison syndrome) as the most likely cause. This patient also has elevated levels of calcium and a family history of nephrolithiasis, which are suggestive of hyperparathyroidism. When all of this is taken into account, we must suspect multiple endocrine neoplasia type I (MEN I). This condition is a constellation of pituitary adenomas, parathyroid tumors, and pancreatic islet cell tumors. Pituitary adenomas secrete prolactin in 25% of patients and growth hormone in 5% of patients. Large pituitary adenomas may cause bitemporal hemianopsia, which is a risk factor for motor vehicle accidents in these patients. Head MRI (choice D) is considered the screening test of choice for pituitary adenomas. → Abdominal CT scan (choice A) in the study of Zollinger-Ellison syndrome is used in the staging of cancer lesion. At this point, it would not be the best next step. → Endoscopic ultrasound with biopsy (choice B) is an invasive study that should not be considered as the next step in the evaluation of this patient. Somatostatin receptor scintigraphy would be the best next step in the evaluation of Zollinger- Ellison syndrome but it was not among the choices offered. → 24-hour urine vanillylmandelic acid (choice C) is useful in evaluating patients suspected of pheochromocytoma. This would be considered in a patient suspected of MEN II. MEN II a is a constellation of pheochromocytoma, parathyroid neoplasia, and medullary carcinoma of the thyroid, while MEN IIb includes pheochromocytoma, medullary thyroid carcinoma, and intestinal neuromas. → Serum calcitonin (choice E) is also useful in the evaluation of medullary carcinoma of the thyroid in patients with MEN II. Key point: Multiple endocrine neoplasia type I is a constellation of pituitary adenomas, parathyroid tumors, and pancreatic islet cell tumors. In a patient who presents with Zollinger-Ellison syndrome and hypercalcemia, a head MRI is indicated to screen the patient for pituitary adenoma.

subject: Medicine
question: A 61-year-old female presents to your department because of sudden vision loss and new onset of headache that is worse at the back of her head. The symptoms started about 6-8 hours ago. She says that she cannot read half of the printed page. Her past medical history is significant for hypercholesterolemia and hypertension. On physical examination left homonymous hemianopsia is noted. Occlusion of which of the following vessels is most likely to be the cause of this condition?
explanation: This patient’s clinical presentation is very concerning for an acute stroke and this is suggested by the symptoms, findings on physical examination and her risk factors. Given her complaints of headaches in the posterior cranium and her vision loss on the left side of each eye (left homonymous hemianopsia), the most likely cause of her condition is an occlusion of the posterior cerebral artery (choice D). The posterior cerebral arteries are paired vessels usually arising from the top of the basilar artery. They supply the occipital lobe of the brain where the primary visual cortex is located. This is why occlusion of both posterior cerebral arteries that results in bilateral infarction of the occipital lobes produces varying degrees of cortical blindness depending on the extent of the lesion. → Temporal artery (choice A) should be thought about in visual disturbances and headaches that are more severe in the temporal region, in an elderly patient with clinical presentation suggestive of giant cell arteritis. → Ophthalmic artery (choice B) occlusion could occur in a patient with risk factors seen in this patient; however, due to circulatory anastomosis, ophthalmic artery occlusion may leave the eye without symptoms. → Lenticulostriate arteries (choice C) originate from the middle cerebral artery and are associated with lacunar stroke. This type of stroke may lead to motor deficits, sensory deficits and mixed motor-sensory deficits. The sensory deficits are usually from thalamus infarction and internal capsules, it would not present with homonymous hemianopsia. → Posterior inferior cerebellar artery (choice E) occlusion leads to the Wallenberg syndrome also known as the lateral medullary syndrome. It is characterized by ipsilateral horner's syndrome due to the descending hypothalamic tracts affected; contralateral loss of pain and temperature due to lateral spinothalamic tract affected; ipsilateral cerebellar ataxia due to cerebellar peduncles affected; and other symptoms especially dysphagia, dysarthria, and dysphonia. Key point: Posterior cerebral artery occlusion can result in homonimous hemianopsia if either the left or right side artery is occluded and can lead to cortical blindness if both arteries are occluded and occipital infarction occurs.

subject: Medicine
question: A 62-year-old male presents to your department complaining of pain in the lower limbs. This is the second visit in the last 3 weeks. Three weeks ago the pain was mostly in the right leg but this time the pain is in the left leg. The patient denies any recent trauma or hospitalization. The patient has lost 3 kg over the last 3 weeks and a total of 8 kg the last 3 months. He drinks alcohol occasionally and has smoked one pack of cigarettes a day for the last 37 years. You note an erythematous nodule on the saphenous vein of the left leg. Palpation reveals a firm, thickened, and possibly thrombosed vein. Which of the following is most likely to confirm the original cause of this patient’s condition?
explanation:
This patient’s symptoms of pain in lower limbs that travels from one leg to another, findings on physical examination of an erythematous nodule of a superficial leg vein that is firm, thickened and possibly thrombosed is suggestive of superficial thrombophlebitis. When it travels from one place to another, it is also known as thrombophlebitis migrans. In this patient, who also presents with 8 kg weight loss over the last 3 months, thrombophlebitis migrans is concerning for malignancy. The most common cancers associated with this condition are pancreatic and lung cancer but it could also be noted in other cancers such as colon and gastric cancers. Thrombophlebitis migrans is also known as Trousseau sign of malignancy. Given the link between this sign and pancreatic cancer, out of the choices given, the best study that would reveal the underlying disease in this patient is abdominal CT scan (choice A). → Peripheral angiography (choice B) would be done to confirm the extent of peripheral artery disease. This patient’s condition is thrombophlebitis migrans. → Ventilation perfusion scan (choice C) is done in patients suspected of pulmonary embolism, which can be a complication of deep vein thrombosis. This patient’s clinical presentation doesn’t suggest pulmonary embolism. → D-dimer test (choice D) is the degradation product of crosslinked fibrin. It reflects ongoing activation of the hemostatic system and is done as a screening test for deep vein thrombosis in patients suspected to have it with low probability. While usually work-up is done in patients with superficial thrombophlebitis to rule out deep vein thrombosis, this question is asking about a study that would confirm the primary cause of this patient’s condition. In the presence of thrombophlebitis migrans, weight loss, and a long history of cigarette smoking, doing an abdominal cancer work up is more appropriate. → Antinuclear antibodies and rheumatoid factor (choice E) are non-specific tests that may be positive in a number of autoimmune and rheumatologic conditions. This patient’s most likely diagnosis is thrombophlebitis migrans caused by a malignant tumor.

Key point: Migratory superficial thrombophlebitis and weight loss in an elderly patient with a long cigarette smoking history is suggestive of malignancy until proven otherwise. Work-up should include abdominal CT scan to rule out pancreatic cancer.

subject: Medicine
question: A 57-year-old male, who had been admitted to your department for management of perforated diverticulitis 48 hour ago, has just suddenly developed a seizure. He has tremors, and is sweating profusely. Vital signs are: temperature 38.6°C, BP is 155/90 mmHg, heart rate is 115 bpm, and respirations are 20/min. After reviewing patient's ED chart, you suspect alcohol withdrawal. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.B: Intravenous hydration with 5% dextrose in water
options.C: 12 doses of 2 mg of lorazepam every 4 hours

correct_answer_text: 12 doses of 2 mg of lorazepam every 4 hours
explanation: This patient’s seizure, tremors, and diaphoresis 48 hours after admission are most likely symptoms of delirium tremens. It is the most severe form of ethanol withdrawal manifested by altered mental status and sympathetic overdrive. This is a medical emergency with high mortality that requires immediate diagnosis and treatment. Benzodiazepines are commonly used in the treatment of delirium tremens, and they are cross-tolerant with alcohol and much safer than other sedatives. If lorazepam is given, initially the best dosage is 12 doses of 2-4 mg of lorazepam every 4 hours (choice C). In case diazepam is given as the choice, it is important to know that 20 mg oral diazepam can be given every 1-2 hours until therapeutically adequate concentrations are reached to improve the clinical condition. if oral diazepam is not tolerated: diazepam 2-5 mg IV/min- maximum 10-20 mg q1h can be given. For patients >65 yrs old or  those with severe liver disease, severe asthma, or respiratory failure, use short acting benzodiazepine such as  lorazepam PO/SL/IM 1-4 mg q1-2h. Please note that diazepam should never be administered intramuscularly as absorption is erratic. → 1mg haloperidol every 8 hours (choice A) is incorrect. Haloperidol is used as an adjunctive therapy in patients who have hallucination or are combative. Benzodiazepines are still the best drugs for the management of delirium tremens. → Intravenous hydration with 5% dextrose in water (choice B) is incorrect. While patients with delirium tremens are often dehydrated and intravenous fluid support is in order, dextrose should not be administered before thiamine is given because there’s a risk of precipitating Wernicke crisis. Normal saline should be given and for hypoglycemic patients 5% dextrose may be added after thiamine has been offered. → Disulfiram, 500 mg per day (choice D) is incorrect. Disulfiram is used to support treatment of alcoholism by inhibiting acetaldehyde dehydrogenase, thus causing an unpleasant reaction when alcohol is consumed. It is not useful in the management of delirium tremens. → 1mg of lorazepam every 6 hours (choice E) is incorrect. This dose would be too little in a patient with delirium tremens. Even in a patient who is calm and cooperative with low risk of delirium tremens, the advised dose is 1 mg of lorazepam every hour. Key point: Delirium is the most severe form of ethanol withdrawal manifested by altered mental status and sympathetic overdrive. It is a medical emergency that is initiall best treated with benzodiazepines. Every 4 hours about 12 doses of 2-4 mg of lorazepam should be given.

subject: Medicine
question: A 17-year-old female is brought to your department by her parents. They found her laying down at home with an acetaminophen bottle next to her. When they asked her what happened she said that she had found out her boyfriend cheated on her with one of her friends. She ingested 25 oral tablets (325mg) that were in the bottle they had recently bought. Assuming the toxicity follows the established stages after this drug ingestion, which of the following findings is least likely to be present in this patient?
explanation: This patient presents after an intentional overdose of acetaminophen. 150 mg/kg or 7.5 g of acetaminophen in adults are considered toxic. This patient has ingested more than 8g. In North America acetaminophen has replaced viral hepatitis as the most common cause of acute hepatic failure and is the second most common cause of liver failure requiring transplantation. Acetaminophen is metabolized in the liver via glucuronidation, sulfation, and through the cytochrome P- 450 pathway. In acute overdose, acetaminophen is oxidatively metabolized to the hepatotoxic reactive metabolite, N- acetyl-p-benzoquinoneimine (NAPQI). The clinical course of acetaminophen toxicity generally is divided into 4 stages: - The first stage that lasts up to 24 hours may be asymptomatic but is usually characterized by anorexia, nausea, vomiting, diaphoresis, pallor, and fatigue. - The second stage follows and goes up to 72 hours post-ingestion. It is characterized by right upper quadrant abdominal pain and tenderness, nausea and vomiting intensify, tachycardia and hypotension are noted. Elevated liver enzymes are found in labs and oliguria with elevated BUN and creatinine may occur. - The third stage also known as hepatic stage is characterized by continued abdominal pain, development of jaundice, coagulopathy, encephalopathy and hypoglycemia. - In patients who survive the fourth stage consists of recovery, which may take up to 21 days. Based on above, the least likely finding is increased serum glucose (choice C) because liver failure results in impaired gluconeogenesis. Hypoglycemia is expected to occur in acetaminophen toxicity. → Increased prothrombin time (choice A), Increased serum aspartate aminotransferase (choice B), Increased bilirubin (choice D) are noticed in the hepatic stage and last for several days before they normalize. → Increased creatinine (choice E) begins with stage 2 and levels greater than 300 µmol/L (3.4 mg/dL), INR of 6.5 and pH < 7.30 should prompt liver transplantation consultation. Key point: Common findings in acetaminophen toxicity are elevated liver enzymes, elevated prothrombin time, elevated bilirubin, elevated BUN and creatinine, and decreased serum glucose.

subject: Medicine
question: Laboratory studies of a 70-year-old male who is being evaluated for abdominal pain reveal hypercalcemia, normal serum phosphorus, and normal calcium levels in urine. Which of the following is most likely to be the diagnosis?
explanation: This patient’s labs demonstrate hypercalcemia, normal serum phosphorus, and normal urine calcium levels in the presence of abdominal pain in an elderly patient, which is suggestive of malignancy (choice B). What is commonly known as the humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy (HHM) in many cancers is associated with parathyroid hormone related peptide (PTHrP), a factor that shares the same receptor with parathyroid hormone but has some differences from this hormone. For this reason its effects should not be confused with what occurs in primary hyperparathyroidism. In humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy, bone formation is suppressed, and patients have a metabolic alkalosis rather than hyperchloremic acidosis. Moreover, serum 1,25 dihydroxyvitamin D3 concentrations are increased in primary hyperparathyroidism and suppressed in cancer. In patients with biochemical findings that suggest but do not prove primary hyperparathyroidism (eg. hypercalcemia, but normal or near normal serum phosphate), HMM should be considered as a diagnostic possibility, particularly if the patient is elderly, has a history of malignancy or risk factors for malignancy. An elevated PTHrP level in such a patient is highly suggestive of HHM as the cause for the hypercalcemia. → Primary hyperparathyroidism (choice A) is associated with hypophosphatemia and hypercalciuria. → Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (choice C) as the name implies, is characterized by a benign hypercalcemia and low calcium level in urine. This patient’s urine calcium is normal, which should exclude this diagnosis. → Paget’s disease (choice D) causes elevated alkaline phosphatase but calcium and phosphate levels should be within normal limits. → Vitamin D intoxication (choice E) would be accompanied by hypercalcemia and hyperphosphatemia as vitamin D increases phosphate reabsorption in the intestines. Key point: Humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy is caused with parathyroid hormone related peptide and can present with hypercalcemia, normal serum phosphorus, and normal urine calcium.

subject: Medicine
question: A 61-year-old male presents to your department because of back pain in the lumbar region of the spine. He describes the pain as gnawing in nature and is rated 9/10. He has tried acetaminophen and ibuprofen unsuccessfully. Recently he has also experienced fatigue and it is making him less productive. The patient denies abdominal pain, vomiting, headaches, and numbness in the lower extremities. He reports losing 5 kg over the last 3 months. He has been constipated for a while, for which he uses stool softeners. On physical examination the patient appears mildly pale, his temperature is 37.8°C, BP 125/ 75 mmHg, pulse 80 bpm, and respirations 15/min. There is tenderness on palpation of the lumbar spine region. The rest of physical examination is unremarkable. Laboratory tests are significant for: ESR 138mm/hr, Hb 104 g/L, MCV 92, Calcium 3.15mmol/L, Alkaline phosphatase 138 U/L, Albumin 31g/L, Serum IgG is decreased. Electrophoresis identified a small paraprotein band and a large amount of free kappa light chains in both the serum and the urine. Which of the following would be most helpful to determine the prognosis of this patient?
explanation:
This patient has a classic presentation of multiple myeloma. This is demonstrated by the lumbar spinal bone pain, 5 kg weight loss, fatigue, constipation most likely caused by elevated calcium as shown by the serum levels 3.15 mmol/l, anemia, elevated ESR, findings of paraproteins and free kappa light chains. Multiple myeloma is a malignancy of plasma cells. Collections of abnormal plasma cells accumulate in the bone marrow where they interfere with the production of normal blood cells. The characteristic monoclonal free light chains in the serum or urine are called Bence Jones proteins. There are two different systems that can be used as staging system and prognostic index of multiple myeloma: The international staging system and the Durie-Salmon system. Currently, the international staging system is preferred for determining the prognosis of multiple myeloma patients. It relies on Beta-2 microglobulin (B2M) levels (choice A) and albumin. Beta-2 microglobulin is a key indicator of tumor burden and the proliferation rate. Under this system stage III multiple myeloma is defined as B2M ≥ 5.5 mg/L. For patients with B2M less than 6 mg/L, the median survival is 54 months (if C-reactive protein also < 6mg/L), and the median survival is 27 months (if C-reactive protein is > 6 mg/L). Using the Durie-Salmon system, poor prognostic factors are: tumor mass, hypercalcemia, Bence Jones proteinemia, advanced lytic bone lesions, and creatinine > 2mg/dL. → Bone scintigraphy uptake (choice B) should not be relied upon in the evaluation of multiple myeloma. Cytokines secreted by multiple myeloma cells suppress osteoblast activity; therefore, typically, no increased uptake is observed. On technetium bone scanning, more than 50% of lesions can be missed. → Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (choice C) is not currently used in determining the prognosis of multiple myeloma. → BCR-ABL gene dysregulation (choice D) is associated with chronic myelogenous leukemia. This patient’s diagnosis is multiple myeloma. → Hepatosplenomegaly (choice E) is present in some patients with multiple myeloma but it is not used as a prognostic index. Key point: Multiple myeloma is characterized by hypercalcemia, renal impairment, anemia, and lytic bone lesions, which cause back pain. Paraproteins, the Bence-Jones proteins are a significant feature of this plasma cell malignancy. Beta-2 microglobulin level is used in determining the prognosis of multiple myeloma.

Multiple Myeloma Multiple Myeloma

subject: Medicine
question: A 41-year-old male who was recently admitted into the hospital after a motor vehicle accident is being evaluated for alcoholic hepatitis. Which of the following lab results would suggest liver disease due to alcohol abuse?
explanation:
Alcoholism is common, serious, and expensive. Besides intoxication and addiction, it is associated with liver cirrhosis, pancreatitis, Wernicke encephalopathy, Korsakoff psychosis, cardiomyopathy, gastrointestinal bleeding, cancers, and fetal alcohol syndrome. In addition, alcohol is involved in 20% of car accidents, 24% of homicides, and 11% of suicides. The diagnosis of an alcohol problem is best achieved through obtaining proper past history. Screening for alcoholism is easy and can be done with the CAGE questionnaire. Indirect alcohol biomarkers are preferred when evaluating long-term alcohol abuse. Patients with alcoholic hepatitis have elevated aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) but the AST level is usually twice higher the level of ALT (AST/ALT > 2). Out of the choices given on this question, only choice D with AST: 210 and ALT: 95, presents an option where AST/ALT > 2. It should be noted that an ALT level above 500 should prompt a physician to consider another possible cause of liver injury than alcohol abuse even if the AST: ALT ratio > 2. → Choices A, B, C, and E can all be seen in patients with liver disease but they are not characteristic of alcoholic liver disease. It is important to note that ALT and AST are better “liver function” indicators than alkaline phosphatase, which is more useful in gallbladder diseases. Alcohol abuse can cause liver hepatitis and this manifests with elevated ALT and AST, where the level of AST is usually

twice higher than the level of ALT.

subject: Medicine
question: A 26-year-old female graduate student who participates in her university female basketball team presents to your department with complaints of right hip pain. She has had the pain for 2 weeks and the pain radiates down the lateral aspect of her right thigh. It is worse when she lies on the right side and when she stands up after sitting for long periods of time. She denies numbness or altered sensation. On examination there is pain on palpation over the lateral hip. Abduction of the hip against resistance reproduces the pain. Internal and external rotation of the hip does not elicit the pain and there’s normal range of movement. When the patient sits with the knee extended and subsequently the right heel is elevated, there’s no pain. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: This patient’s most likely diagnosis is trochanteric bursitis (choice A). It is a painful inflammation of the bursa located just superficial to the greater trochanter of the femur. The pain may radiate down the lateral aspect of the ipsilateral thigh; however, it should not radiate all the way into the foot. The pain worsens when the patient lies on the affected bursa. It is characterized by pain on palpation of the lateral portion of the hip with normal internal and external rotation. → Iliopsoas tendinitis (choice B) is incorrect. In this condition, on physical examination, there’s an anterior pelvic tilt on palpation due to tightening of the iliopsoas muscle. There’s also pain when the patient sits with extended knees and the heel on the affected is subsequently elevated. This is known as Ludloff sign and is negative in this patient. → Polymyalgia rheumatic (choice C) is characterized by proximal myalgia of the hip and shoulder girdles with accompanying morning stiffness that lasts for more than 1 hour. 50% of patients with temporal arteritis have polymyalgia rheumatica. Patients are older than 50 years of age and there is decreased active range of motion. → Osteoarthritis (choice D) similarly to trochanteric bursitis is associated with strenuous activities and the pain worsens with activity. Reduced range of motion and crepitus are almost always present. → Avascular necrosis (choice E) is incorrect. In this condition both active and passive joint movements may be restricted and painful and neurologic deficits are present unlike trochanter bursitis. Key point: Trochanteric bursitis is characterized by painful inflammation of the bursa located just superficial to the greater trochanter of the femur. Physical exam reveals pain on palpation of the lateral portion of the hip with normal internal and external rotation.

subject: Medicine
question: A 37-year-old female presents to your department because complaining of nausea and vomiting for the last 3 days. She has also been having headaches. Physical examination is only remarkable for abdominal distension and BP 165/100 mmHg. Her BP has been high the last 3 months despite treatment with amlodipine that was started at 5 mg once a day and was later increased to 10 mg once a day. Comprehensive metabolic panel reveals: BUN: 7 mmol/L Creatinine: 80 micromol/L Calcium: 2.40 mmol/L Chloride: 96 mmol/L Bicarbonate: 31 mmol/L Glucose test: 5 mmol/L Potassium test: 2.7 mmol/L Sodium: 148 mmol/L Albumin: 42 g/L What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
This patient is presenting with a history of hypertension that is not responding to calcium channel blockers and has non- specific symptoms like nausea and vomiting. The major clue to the cause of this patient’s condition  is the laboratory tests results that show hypokalemia and mild hypernatremia. These electrolyte abnormalities are associated with hyperaldosteronism and given the history of resistant hypertension, the patient’s most likely diagnosis is Conn’s syndrome (choice C). Other aspects of clinical presentation that may be noted are weakness, abdominal distention, Ileus from hypokalemia (which can cause nausea and vomiting), findings related to complications of hypertension such as cardiac failure, hemiparesis due to stroke, carotid bruits, abdominal bruits, proteinuria, renal insufficiency, and hypertensive encephalopathy. → Liver cirrhosis (choice A) may cause abdominal distension and vomiting with portal hypertension and ascites and even hypokalemia. Hypokalemia in liver cirrhosis is usually multifactorial and may be associated with diuretics use, magnesium depletion in alcoholics, vomiting, and secondary hyperaldosteronism. However, this patient’s scenario doesn’t present risk factors of liver cirrhosis and primary aldosteronism is far more common than secondary aldosteronism. → Cushing's syndrome (choice B) can also cause hypertension and even hypokalemia with extremely high levels of cortisol. However, it would also cause findings often remarkable on physical examination such as facial plethora, hirsutism, buffalo hump, etc. → Pheochromocytoma (choice D) presents with episodes of severe hypertension due catecholamine secretion. Other classic 3 symptoms are diaphoresis, palpitations, and headaches. It may be associated with multiple endocrine neoplasia type II. Hypernatremia and hypokalemia are more likely to be seen with elevated aldosterone secretion than with

increased catecholamine secretions. → Addison’s disease (choice E) is adrenal insufficiency and would cause the inverse of what is noted in this patient, with hypotension, hyponatremia, and hyperkalemia being the major findings. Key point: Hyperaldosteronism such as seen in Conn's syndrome is associated with hypertension, hypernatremia, and hypokalemia.

subject: Medicine
question: A 19-year-old male presents to your department because of abdominal pain for the last 2 days. The pain is localized in the right lower quadrant and he rates it as 7 out of 10. He also complains of diarrhea and loss of appetite. His past medical history is non-remarkable. His family history is significant for a father with hemochromatosis. On physical examination, the patient’s skin appears bronzing, he has tenderness on palpation of the right lower quadrant and rebound tenderness is also noted. The Rovsing sign and psoas sign are negative. Abdominal CT scan demonstrates enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes, ileocecal wall thickening, and a normal appearing appendix. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
This patient has right lower quadrant abdominal pain, diarrhea, and anorexia. His skin appears bronzing and given his family history of hemochromatosis, he is likely to also have this disease. The above symptoms and physical examination findings when combined with the findings on CT scan that shows enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes, ileocecal wall thickening, and a normal appearing appendix suggest mesenteric lympadenitis. This is an inflammation of the mesenteric lymph nodes that may be acute or chronic depending on etiology. While E coli and other infectious agents could cause mesenteric lymphadenitis, in this patient with hemochromatosis, Yersiniosis (choice A) caused by Yersinia enterocolitica is the most likely etiology. It is an iron loving, non-lactose fermenting, and oxidase-negative facultative anaerobe. Iron overload that is characteristic of hemochromatosis patients is considered a thriving environment for these bacteria. → Epiploic appendagitis (choice B) is a rare disease that results from torsion of the epiploic appendages, which presents as an acute clinical condition mimicking diverticulitis, appendicitis, or other more serious causes of acute abdominal pain. This patient’s CT scan findings are more consistent with mesenteric lymphadenitis. In epiploic appendagitis, the most common finding on CT is a fat-density oval lesion with surrounding inflammation on the anterior aspect of the sigmoid colon. → Appendicitis (choice C) is incorrect. While this patient’s symptoms of right lower quadrant abdominal pain and the findings of rebound tenderness when the right lower quadrant is palpated are also seen in appendicitis, the negative Rovsing sign, psoas sign, and the CT scan findings point to a diagnosis of mesenteric lymphadenitis. → Ulcerative colitis (choice D) is a chronic inflammatory bowel disease that would most likely present with rectal

bleeding. CT scan has limited role in the diagnosis of uncomplicated ulcerative colitis but would be useful in the diagnosis of its complications such as toxic megacolon. This patient’s CT findings point to mesenteric lymphadenitis. → E coli mesenteric lymphadenitis (choice E) is incorrect. While this patient’s clinical picture certainly fits the diagnosis of mesenteric lymphadenitis, given his hemochromatosis family history and the bronzing skin, Yersinia enterocolitica, is the more likely causative agent, as it is a well known iron-loving bacteria. Key point: Right lower quadrant abdominal pain, tenderness on palpation, and  CT scan findings of enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes, ileocecal wall thickening, and a normal appearing appendix suggest mesenteric lymphadenitis. In a patient with hemochromatosis, Yersinia enterocolitica is the most causative agent of mesenteric lymphadenitis.

subject: Medicine
question: A 37-year-old male presents to your department with complaints of headache, fever, and vomiting for 3 days. He has used acetaminophen, which has had minimal effect. Past medical history is non-remarkable. He has smoked 50 packs of cigarettes a year for the last 10 years. On physical examination his vital signs are temperature 38.9°C, BP 150/95 mmHg, pulse 110 bpm, and respiration 18/min. The patient exhibits a petechial rash on both arms and the chest. Neck stiffness is also noted on examination. What is the most appropriate next step in the work up of this patient?
explanation:
This patient presents with the meningitis triad of fever, headache, and nuchal rigidity. For patients in this age group and the risk factors (only smoking), the most likely infectious agents would be Streptococcus pneumonia and Neisseria meningitidis. In addition to symptoms suggestive of meningitis, the patient also has a petechial rash commonly associated with meningococcemia. The gold standard for the diagnosis of systemic meningococcal infection is the isolation of N. meningitidis by culture from a usually sterile body fluid, such as blood or cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), or, less commonly, synovial, pleural, or pericardial fluid. Perform lumbar puncture (LP) (choice D) for CSF evaluation. Gram stain of the CSF should be performed immediately and examined microscopically. Organisms can be observed in the CSF in approximately half of patients who present with meningococcal meningitis. → Head CT scan (choice A) before a LP are unnecessary unless the patient is obtunded, has focal neurologic signs, has experienced a seizure within the previous week, or presents with papilledema. → Funduscopic exam (choice B) is another way to detect papilledema, which is associated with increased risks of brain herniation when lumbar puncture is performed. While in the early stage of papilledema the vision is unaffected, with prolonged papilledema, patients experience visual disturbances such as diplopia. Since this patient is most likely to have

meningococcemia and LP should be done. → Coagulation profile (choice C) is indicated in cases of chronic alcohol use, chronic liver disease, or suspected disseminated intravascular coagulation. The best next step in this patient is LP. → The polymerase chain reaction (PCR) (choice E) is a sensitive and rapid tool for diagnosing meningococcal infection. However, PCR has not replaced traditional culture methods because it cannot be used to determine antimicrobial susceptibility and is not routinely performed by most hospital laboratories. Key point: Fever, headache, and nuchal rigidity form the meningitis triad. A patient suspected for meningitis who also has a petechial rash most likely has meningococcal meningitis. The gold standard for the diagnosis of systemic meningococcal infection is the isolation of N. meningitidis by culture from a usually sterile body fluid, such as blood or cerebrospinal fluid.

subject: Medicine
question: A 37-year-old female presents to your department with a complaint of severe chest pain underneath her sternum. She rates the pain as 8/10 and has had it for the last seven days. It gets worse when she lies down and when she bends over and has been relieved with ranitidine. She has no difficulty swallowing and no shortness of breath. She is getting concerned and wants your help. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
This patient presents with retrosternal chest pain. The differential diagnosis of patients presenting with chest pain is extensive, ranging from benign musculoskeletal etiologies to life-threatening cardiac disease. This patient is relatively young, and her chest pain is worsened by laying down and gets better with ranitidine. It is most likely to be caused by gastroesophageal reflux (choice C). It occurs when the gastric acid that refluxes into the esophagus exceeds the normal limit, causing symptoms with or without associated esophageal mucosal injury (esophagitis). → Costochondritis (choice A) presents with chest wall pain with a history of repeated minor trauma or unaccustomed activity such as moving furniture. It may be exacerbated by deep inspiration and decreased with quiet breathing. NSAIDs are first line in the management of costochondritis. This patient’s relief of chest pain with ranitidine suggests a different diagnosis. → Unstable angina (choice B) belongs to the spectrum known as acute coronary syndrome, differentiated from myocardial infarction by absence of release of the enzymes and biomarkers of myocardial necrosis. While it occurs at rest just as seen in this patient, it is best managed with aspirin and beta-blockers; the effectiveness of ranitidine in this patient suggests a different diagnosis. → Prinzmetal angina (choice D) is a temporary increase in coronary vascular tone (vasospasm) causing a marked, but transient reduction in luminal diameter. This coronary vasospastic state is usually focal at a single site and can occur in

either a normal or diseased vessel. Patients are predominantly younger women who may not have the classical cardiovascular risk factors (except for cigarette use). Until atherosclerotic coronary disease is excluded, the initial treatment includes nitrates, beta-blockers, and anti-thrombotic agents. Once the diagnosis is confirmed, it is best treated with calcium channel blockers. This patient’s improvement with ranitidine suggests a different diagnosis. → Achalasia (choice E) is a primary esophageal motility disorder characterized by the absence of esophageal peristalsis and impaired lower esophageal sphincter relaxation in response to swallowing. It could present in a similar fashion as seen in this patient as heartburn is common in patients with achalasia. However, dysphagia is a significant symptom seen in majority of patients and the fact it is not present in this patient should make us think of a different diagnosis. It is also important to note that GERD is a much more common disease than achalasia. Key point: Retrosternal chest pain in a patient without significant risk factors for cardiovascular disease that gets worse with lying down and improves with ranitidine suggests gastroesophageal reflux disease.

subject: Medicine
question: A 48-year-old male presents to your department because he has had pressure-like sensation in the upper abdomen for the last 3 weeks with abdominal pain that worsens with eating food. The pain sometimes radiates to the chest. Physical examination reveals upper abdominal tenderness on deep palpation. In the course of work up an endoscopy with biopsy is performed and reveals gastritis with Helicobacter pylori infection. What is the best treatment regimen to eradicate this infection?
explanation:
This patient is diagnosed with gastritis secondary to Helicobacter pylori infection. It usually presents with abdominal pain that worsens with food intake, heartburn or esophageal reflex, diarrhea, nausea and vomiting. Various tests can be used to make the diagnosis including esophagogastroduodenoscopy, H. pylori fecal antigen test, and H. pylori serology. Treatment should be given to patients with positive results. Treatment with triple therapy should be administered for 10- 14 days. The treatment regimens are omeprazole, amoxicillin, and clarithromycin (OAC) (choice E) - for 10 days; bismuth subsalicylate, metronidazole, and tetracycline (BMT) for 14 days; and lansoprazole, amoxicillin, and clarithromycin (LAC), which is approved for either 10 days or 14 days of treatment. 4 weeks after treatment, carbon-13 urea breath test should be done to confirm eradication. → Clarithromycin, omeprazole, and fluconazole (choice A) is incorrect. Fluconazole, an antifungal is not part of the treatment regimen to eradicate bacteria. → A combination of erythromycin, esomeprazole, and metronidazole (choice B) has greater likelihood of failure, given erythromycin decreased efficacy in acid environment. Its derivative, clarithromycin is more acid-resistant and is the preferred macrolide in H. pylori eradication.

→ Amoxicillin-clavulanate, ranitidine, and bismuth (choice C) is incorrect. Most tested regimens that have amoxicillin also include clarithromycin, moreover, PPI are stronger acid inhibitors than antihistamines. → Bismuth, omeprazole, and metronidazole (choice D) is incorrect. Most tested regimens with metronidazole also include either tetracycline or clarithromycin. Key point: For H. pylori eradication the most common regimens are omeprazole, amoxicillin, and clarithromycin (OAC) for 10 days; bismuth subsalicylate, metronidazole, and tetracycline (BMT) for 14 days; and lansoprazole, amoxicillin, and clarithromycin (LAC), which is approved for either 10 days or 14 days of treatment.
